'''Nicholas Kratzer''' (1487? – 1550), also known as Nicolaus Kratzer and Nicholas Crutcher, was a German [[mathematician]], astronomer, and [[horologist]]. Much of Kratzer's professional life was spent in England, where he was appointed as astronomer to King [[Henry VIII of England|Henry VIII]].

==Life==
Born in [[Munich]] in 1486 or 1487,<ref>{{Cite ODNB|id=15808|title=Kratzer, Nicolaus (b. 1486/7, d. after 1550)}}</ref> Kratzer was the son of a saw-smith, and was educated at the Universities of [[University of Cologne|Cologne]] (B.A. 1509) and [[Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg|Wittenberg]]. He came to England in 1516 and established himself as part of the artistic and scientific circle around Sir [[Thomas More]].<ref name=North>{{cite book | first = J.D. | last = North | chapter = Nicolaus Kratzer – The King's Astronomer | title = Science and History: Studies in Honour of Edward Rosen (Ossolinium Orbis, 1978) | pages = 205–234 | date = 1978 | publisher = Studia Copernica}} Reprinted in: {{cite book | first = J.D. | last = North | title = Stars, Minds and Fate. Essays in Ancient and Medieval Cosmology | pages = 373–400 | place = London | publisher = The Hambledon Press | date = 1989 | isbn = 978-0-907628-94-1}}</ref> Kratzer tutored More's children in mathematics and astronomy and More introduced him at court in much the same way as he had their mutual friend [[Hans Holbein the Younger|Hans Holbein]], who produced [[Portrait of Nicolaus Kratzer|a portrait of Kratzer]]. In the same manner as Holbein, Kratzer's talents obtained him a court position as astronomer and clock maker to the king.
[[File:Fowler Corpus Christi Kratzer's dial.jpg | thumb | 150px | left | Sundial by Kratzer, formerly in the garden of [[Corpus Christi College, Oxford]].<ref name=Fowler/>]]

Kratzer was the designer of a painted ceiling featuring the zodiac and the seven planets which was installed in a temporary banqueting house erected at [[Greenwich Palace]] in March 1527. According to accounts kept by Richard Gibson, an officer of the revels, "Master Nikolas" worked with the painter "Master Hans", Hans Holbein, and was paid 4 shillings a day.<ref>[[Sydney Anglo]], ''Spectacle Pageantry and Early Tudor Policy'' (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1969), pp. 218–219.</ref>

Kratzer also collaborated with Holbein on producing maps, and in return the artist produced a portrait of Kratzer in 1528 that now hangs in the [[Louvre]]; it depicts the craftsman surrounded by the tools of his trade, and with an unfinished polyhedral [[sundial]]. His close relationship with Holbein and More also may be observed in his annotations of Holbein's draft for his portrait of the More family.<ref>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/entertainment/5381412.stm BBC News article on Holbein's draft of the More portrait, with Kratzer's annotations]</ref> Kratzer identifies the various family members and their ages for the benefit of More's friend, the theologian [[Desiderius Erasmus|Erasmus]].

Kratzer (under the name Nich. Cratcherus) is recorded as a reader of [[Corpus Christi College, Oxford]], where he is presumed to have taught mathematics.<ref name = Fowler>{{cite book | first = Thomas | last = Fowler | title = The History of Corpus Christi College | date = 1893 | publisher = Oxford Historical Society | url = https://archive.org/details/histcorpuschristi00fowluoft}}. See in particular pp 84–7.</ref> He designed at least two fixed sundials in Oxford, both of which are now lost. One was in [[University Church of St Mary the Virgin|St Mary's]] churchyard,<ref>[[:File:Loggan Oxonia St Mary's Church, Kratzer's Dial, published 1675.jpg]]</ref> the other in the garden of [[Corpus Christi College, Oxford|Corpus Christi]].<ref name=Fowler/> He also designed a portable dial for Cardinal Wolsey, which is now in the [[History of Science Museum, Oxford]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://hsm.ox.ac.uk/collections-online#/item/hsm-catalogue-2978 | title=Polyhedral Dial, by Nicolaus Kratzer?, English, 1518–30 | website=HSM Collections Online | publisher=History of Science Museum | id=Inventory Number 54054}}</ref> Another dial attributed to Kratzer was found at [[Acton Court]], near Bristol, in the 1980s.<ref>{{cite journal | first = G. S. J. | last = White | title =  A stone polyhedral sundial dated 1520, attributed to Nicholas Kratzer and found at Iron Acton Court, near Bristol | journal = Antiquaries Journal | volume = 67 | date = 1987}}</ref><ref>[https://mercuriuspoliticus.wordpress.com/2011/08/03/acton-court/ Description of Acton Court with a picture of the stone sundial]</ref>

Peter Drinkwater has presented a critical evaluation of the sundials attributed to Kratzer, in particular the one in the Holbein portrait.<ref>{{cite journal | first = Peter | last = Drinkwater | title = A cold look at Kratzer's "polyhedral" sundial | journal = BSS Bulletin | volume = 93 | issue = 2 | pages = 8–10, 20 | publisher = British Sundial Society | date = 1993}}</ref> He comments that "Kratzer triumphed, not through genius or creativity, but through having learned what others had discovered and invented, and by being the first to apply that learning in England". [[John North (historian)|John North]] concurs: "Kratzer doubtless had nothing new to offer of a fundamental kind. Many of his dials were unusual, but his favorite polyhedral dial was perhaps more useful as a repository of verses [...] than for actually announcing the time with any accuracy". Nonetheless, Kratzer brought useful German skills and knowledge to the English court and was well-regarded over a period of nearly 30 years.<ref name = North/>
